claims.rule: Every surface of an action (its CLI command, MCP and WebMCP tools, web control, App Intent, SwiftUI button and Reins action) is generated from one defineAction declaration.
claims.why: Declared four times, one action's surfaces disagree, and an agent and a person see different products.
claims.check: An app's actions file passes defineActions, and its generated folder passes `node ouro-actions.mts check`.
claims.fix: Declare the action with defineAction, add it to the set, run generate, and build the surface from the generated file.

claims.rule: Every committed projection equals what its declaration generates, and a live MCP server's tools/list equals the declared tools; CI fails on any difference.
claims.why: A surface that drifts from its declaration lets an agent do what a person can't, or the reverse, without anyone seeing it.

evidence.finding: WebKit opposes WebMCP partly because a separate agent layer lets agent and human abilities drift apart; a check that fails on drift is the answer.

claims.check: `node ouro-actions.mts check <actions.mts> <dir>` and `node ouro-actions.mts compare-mcp <actions.mts> <tools.json>` in the app's CI; core's own CI runs `pnpm actions:check` on the shopping fixture (test/actions.test.mts proves both checks fail on drift).
claims.fix: Change the declaration and run generate; never edit a generated file, and serve MCP tools from mcp.json.

claims.rule: A person-only action has no agent door: the CLI refuses its words, MCP and WebMCP don't list it and answer a call with the typed refusal (outcome refused, code person-only, exit 2, its reason and how the person does it), web's component AX declares it personOnly, and it has no App Intent.
claims.why: An agent that can start what only the person may start, such as paying or turning on their microphone, acts in their name without their say.

evidence.finding: Apple's ToolIntent guidance (iOS 27.3 beta) lists intents with side effects a person needs to start explicitly, such as placing an order and paying for it, as poor tools.

claims.check: test/actions.test.mts ("the generated JSON lists person-only actions only as refusals, on every agent door") and ("Swift: one App Intent per agent door, ...": no App Intent for a person-only action), and apple/actions-check (OuroActions.refusal(for:) answers with web's code, exit and message).
claims.fix: Declare the action consent "person-only" with personOnly { reason, how }, and run generate.

claims.rule: A consequential action is prepared by the agent and committed by the person: web's effect is "others" (web's kit then requires --why and previews with --dry-run), MCP marks it destructive and open-world, WebMCP marks it consequential, and its App Intent asks requestConfirmation() before it acts.
claims.why: An effect other people see, or one that can't be taken back, must not happen on an agent's say alone.

evidence.finding: Apple's requestConfirmation() is the guard before performing any work that might be destructive or unsafe; WebMCP's consequentialHint and UCP's requires_escalation (https://ucp.dev/latest/specification/shopping/checkout/) serve the same purpose on the web.

claims.check: test/actions.test.mts (consent classes onto annotations, the CLI's effect, and requestConfirmation only in the consequential intent).
claims.fix: Declare the action consent "consequential" and run generate.

claims.rule: Each action carries an agent description, one line written for a model, apart from the person's label and description; the agent doors use it and the person's controls don't.
claims.why: A model chooses a tool and fills its parameters from its description; a button's two words don't tell it when to use the action.

evidence.finding: Siri tells intents apart and fills their parameters from the title and description on each intent and parameter.

claims.check: defineAction refuses an action without a one-line agent description.
claims.fix: agent: "<when to use it and what it does, for a model>".
